title: Revelation, looking back
hookLine: a Lamb on a throne, a city with open gates
tomorrow: what do you say when someone's world falls apart?

lines: ONE TAP, AND A DOOR IS SHUT.
JOHN TURNS TO SEE THE LION.
cards: Somebody leaves the group chat, and a small gray line says so. One tap, and a door is shut. Revelation is a book of doors, and of one scroll nobody can open.

In John's vision he is weeping, because no one in heaven or on earth is worthy to open the sealed scroll. An elder tells him to stop crying: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has prevailed. So John turns to look at the lion.

teach.b: Here's what he sees: "in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain." He was told lion. He sees a wounded lamb.
That swap is a key to the whole book.
Revelation is crowded with beasts, trumpets and fire, and Christians read it in different ways: some as a map of the future, some as a picture of the struggles of John's own day, some as both.
But at the center, on the throne, power looks like love that has been wounded.
Something to tell a friend tonight: it's Revelation, singular. Its first words call it "The Revelation of Jesus Christ." And it ends in a city.
A voice from the throne says, "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things.
All things, new: the old ones, made over. Tears are on the list: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."
Then the gates: "the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there."

City gates are built to close at dark. These have no dark to close for. Looking back, that's where the Bible's long story lands: not an escape from the world, but the world made over, with the gates left open.

how: Some churches read Revelation 21 at funerals and in seasons of hope, and some Christians read the book slowly in study groups, a few chapters at a time.

s: the book's name is Revelations, plural
its first words: 'The Revelation of Jesus Christ.' one revelation, singular.
told a lion has won, John turns and sees a Lamb as it had been slain
Revelation 5:5–6: the lion he's promised is a wounded lamb.
'I make all things new' means God throws the old world away and starts over
the line says all things, new: the old ones made over, tears wiped away.

games.q: you're John, weeping over a sealed scroll. an elder says the Lion of Judah has prevailed. you turn to look. what's there?
o: a lion, roaring, on the throne.
a Lamb as it had been slain.
games.why: he's told lion and sees a wounded lamb, standing in the midst of the throne. at the center of a book of beasts and trumpets, power looks like wounded love.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one door you've shut: on a person, a hope, or a part of yourself. You don't have to walk through it.
For these two minutes, let it stand open a crack, and let whatever light is on the other side simply be there.

wordCard.voice: Revelation. Beasts and trumpets at the edges, a slain Lamb at the center, and a city whose gates never shut.

orig.note: Greek: new. the word behind 'I make all things new' in Revelation 21:5.
